title: What is price elasticity, and how do you use it in a pricing case?
description: Price elasticity explained simply, with a worked example of whether a price rise increases revenue and profit, and how to talk about it in a case.
hook: Every pricing case hides the same question: if we change the price, how many customers will we lose or gain? Price elasticity is the name for that relationship, and a few simple numbers tell you whether a price change helps or hurts.
body:
The idea

Elasticity = % change in volume ÷ % change in price. If a 10% price rise loses 5% of volume, elasticity is −0.5: demand is fairly insensitive. If it loses 20%, elasticity is −2: very sensitive.

A worked example

A product sells 100,000 units at £10, costing £6 each to make. Revenue £1M, profit £400k.

Raise the price 10% to £11. If volume falls 5% to 95,000: revenue £1.045M, profit 95,000 × £5 = £475k, up 19%. If volume falls 20% to 80,000: revenue £880k, profit 80,000 × £5 = £400k, unchanged.

The break-even volume loss

Margin per unit rises from £4 to £5. Profit stays the same while volume × £5 = £400k, so volume can fall to 80,000, a 20% loss, before the price rise stops paying. Higher margins make price rises safer.

What affects elasticity

  • Close substitutes make demand more sensitive.
  • Essentials and habits make it less sensitive.
  • Switching costs and contracts reduce sensitivity in the short term.

How to say it

A 10% price rise pays off as long as we lose fewer than 20% of customers. Given few close substitutes, I'd expect much less, so I'd test it in one region first.
